intro: KUB 7.8 with its joins (KUB 9.27 and KUB 7.5) preserves the ritual of Paškuwatti, a woman of Arzawa living in Parša, for a man who lacks procreative power or 'is not a man towards a woman' (CTH 406). The patient passes through gates of reed, handing over spindle and distaff in exchange for bow and arrows. Then comes a three-day cycle of prayers and offerings to the deity Uliliyašši, during which he sleeps before the offering table in the hope that the god will come to him in a dream. The end of the tablet is lost.

paras.en: Thus (says) Paškuwatti, woman of Arzawa, who lives in Parša: If some man has no procreative power, or is not a man with respect to a woman,

I make offerings to Uliliyašši for him and entreat him for three days. On the first day I do as follows: one soldier-bread is piled up(?), and below it this is arranged: three thick loaves of moist, sweet flour of a tarna-measure; figs, raisins, kallaktar (a cereal food?), parḫuena-(grain), the god's groats, a little of each; tufts of ewe's wool; [one] jug of wine; and also that man's, the offerant's, [BAR.TE]-garments or GÚ.È.A-shirt. They lie on the soldier-bread.

A virgin girl lifts them up, while the offerant, [ba]thed, walks behind (her). […] bathed(?). We carry them to a fresh place in the open country and set (them down). The [same girl] holds the soldier-bread lifted up, and I make gates of reed.

[The]n I bind them with red wool (and) white wool. I put a spindle and a distaff into the offerant's [hand], and he passes [through] beneath the gates. When he steps [ou]t of the gates, I take the spindle and the distaff away from him and give him a bow [(and) arrows], and meanwhile I speak as follows: 'See, I have taken femininity away from you and given you masculinity in its place. You have cast off the ways [of a woman]; [you have taken] up the ways of a man!'

Then forth … […] … and […], and meanwhile I sp[eak as follows]: […] 'See, (to) you […]' [gap of about six lines] '… and to him … (ḫattarša-?) […] … lies(?), or a pure maiden …-ed, and went down into his andakitti- (inner chamber?). And this mortal child, (a thing) of dung (and) urine, did not find you.

But now, see, he has come back down after (you) … (kinuwašša-, meaning unclear), and he keeps seeking after you, O god, in (your) divinity(?). Whether (you are) on the mountain, whether in the meadow, whether in the valley, or wherever (you may be), come with good (intent) to this person! Let neither winds(?) nor rains beat against your eyes!

He will proceed to make you (his) god: he will present you a place, he will give you a house, he will give you a male servant (and) a female servant, he will give you cattle (and) sheep, and he will make you a maltešnala- (votive offering?).

See, I keep entreating you and calling on you. So come! Bring the Moon-god, the Star(s) (and) the Sun-goddess of the Earth along with you. Let (your) female and male servants run before (you); let your male gods [and female gods] run before (you). Come to this person! (As for) a son for him and his wife(?) — you look after him! Turn to him and speak to him! Allot him your female servant, and let her become a yoke(-mate) for him. Let him take (her as) his wife, and let him beget sons and daughters for himself. And they (will be) your male servants (and) female servants, and they will keep giving you those offerings: ḫaršau-breads, groats (and) išpantuzziyaššar-libation vessels.

See, this person did not know you, but now, see, he has sought after you. And just as this one has sought after you, (so) you, O god, step in to him with good (intent)! And in the matter for which we keep entreating you here on earth(?), show (your) divinity, O god, and make it good! Let him look up to [your] [divi]nity! He will come and make you the [god] o[f his (own) person].' [gap of about seven lines] And I place the [broken] [thick loaves](?) back on the soldier-bread, and we go back home. In whichever house I perform the ritual, a new table is set up, and I place the soldier-bread on the table, and below in front of it I place the jug.

Of the broken thick loaves which lie on the soldier-bread I take a little and give it to the man, the offerant, and he puts it in his mouth and drinks three times (to) Uliliyašši. When it becomes evening, the offerant sleeps right in front of the table; they set his bed down right in front of the table.

The BAR.TE-garments or GÚ.È.A-shirt which lie on the soldier-bread he spreads out beneath (himself) at night. I perform it for three days, and in one day I entreat three times: in the morning; in the middle of the day, once; at evening time, once. And in (each prayer) I keep speaking those same words. And the thick loaves

which I break in the morning — at midday I break other thick loaves, and at evening time I break other (ones), and I also pour out other groats. Then I offer one sheep to Uliliyašši, and they slaughter it down in front of the table. They carry the sheep out and [cu]t it (up); then […] […]; then the meat […] […] the breast, the shoulder […] […] and they place it on the table […]. The liver [(and) the heart] they cook [on an open flam]e […] … two(?) thick loaves […] … on the table […]
[…] cuts […] […] of the broken (loaves) […] … […] […] [Ulil]iyašši […] […] the Moon-god, the stars […] […] …

[…] good […] gods […] to the god […] … […] as follows […] [gap of about five lines] […] back […] 'You, allot him [your female servant], and let her become a yoke(-mate) for him. Let him take (her as) his wife, let him beget his children, let him beget sons and daughters! And you, O god, show (your) divinity!

And let him see (your) majesty! He will make you, O god, (the god) of his (own) person; he will make you a maltešnala- (votive offering?).' Then they spread out the bed for him once more right in front of the table, and the BAR.TE-garments or GÚ.È.A-shirt which lie on the soldier-bread, those too they spread beneath him. Then the offerant lies down to sleep. If he sees the god in a dream in person(?) (lit. 'in his body') — (if) he goes to him and sleeps with him — (then), while I entreat the god for three days, he keeps telling the dreams that he sees: whether the god keeps revealing (his) eyes to him, (and) whether the god sleeps with him.

Then he comes and makes (him his) god. Moreover, if a ḫaršiyalli-storage jar is suitable for him, he sets him (the god) up as a ḫaršiyalli-storage jar; but if not, he sets him up as a ḫuwaši-stele, or else he makes him a statue. And the new table which stood (there) at the invocation becomes the god's own.
But if he does [not see] (him) in person(?), [and] the god does [not sleep] with him in a dream, I keep on performing (the ritual).
